IB Chemistry HL
Dipole Moment and Electronegativity of Hydrides

How do I use this resource?

a

medium

Deduce the electron domain geometry and the molecular shape of hydrogen selenide, HX2Se.\ce{H2Se}.HX2​Se. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

a

Mark Scheme

electron domain geometry: tetrahedral ✓\checkmark✓
molecular shape: bent / V–\text{--}–shaped ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The Lewis structure of HX2Se\ce{H2Se}HX2​Se should have 2×1+6=82\times 1 + 6 = 82×1+6=8 valence electrons. Selenium is the central atom with single bonds to the two hydrogen atoms and two nonbonding pairs on the selenium atom.

There are four electron domains around selenium: two bonding and two nonbonding pairs. According to the valence shell electron pair repulsion theory (VSEPR), the electron domain geometry is tetrahedral to maximize the distance between the electron pairs. Since two are nonbonding pairs, the shape of the molecule is bent or V–\text{--}–shaped.

 \  

b

medium

Explain the trend in boiling points of the Group 14 hydrides: CHX4,\ce{CH4},CHX4​, SiHX4,\ce{SiH4},SiHX4​, GeHX4,\ce{GeH4},GeHX4​, and SnHX4\ce{SnH4}SnHX4​ in Table 1. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

b

Mark Scheme

nonpolar molecules are attracted London dispersion forces which increase with molecular mass / molecular size / number of electrons ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The boiling points of the Group 14 hydrides increase down the group. This is because as you move down Group 14 the molecular mass increases, leading to stronger London dispersion forces (temporary dipole–\text{--}–induced dipole interactions). Larger atoms have more electrons, making them more polarizable, which further strengthens these intermolecular forces.

Since boiling point is determined by the strength of intermolecular forces, more energy is required to overcome the stronger London dispersion forces in heavier hydrides, leading to a higher boiling point.

c

medium

Explain the trend in the dipole moment of the Group 17 hydrides: HF, HCl, HBr and HI using Section 9 of the IB Chemistry data booklet and the data in Table 1. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

c

Mark Scheme

electronegativity difference decreases down group ✓\checkmark✓
partial charges are smaller, bond dipole is weaker ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The dipole moment of the Group 17 hydrides decreases down the group. The dipole moment is directly related to the difference in electronegativity between hydrogen and the halogen. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so HF has the most polar bond and the largest dipole moment.

Moving down the group, the electronegativity of the halogen decreases, reducing the bond polarity and thus the dipole moment.

d

medium

Suggest an explanation for the high boiling point of water compared to ammonia, NHX3,\ce{NH3},NHX3​, and hydrogen fluoride, HF,\ce{HF},HF, in Table 1. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

d

Mark Scheme

water forms four strong intermolecular interactions, while HF and NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​ form only two ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
In water, the geometry allows the molecule to be a hydrogen bond acceptor to two adjacent molecules and a hydrogen bond donor to another two adjacent hydrogen bonds.

Water acts as both a donor and acceptor for two bonds, forming a highly interconnected network of strong hydrogen bonding. The hydrogen bonds are oriented on a line through a lone pair on the acceptor molecule to the O−H\ce{O-H}O−H bond on the donor molecule.

In ammonia, only one hydrogen can be used as a hydrogen bond donor and the single lone pair can accept one hydrogen bond. Similarly, in hydrogen fluoride, only one lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond and the single hydrogen can be a hydrogen bond donor. There is a balance between the number of total acceptors and donors in the liquid.

 \

strength: trend is correct for PHX3,\ce{PH3},PHX3​, HX2S,\ce{H2S},HX2​S, and HCl\ce{HCl}HCl ✓\checkmark✓
weakness: phosphine has a dipole moment and 0% ionicity ✓\checkmark✓

There is a general trend that increasing percent ionicity corresponds to increasing dipole moment, However, SiHX4\ce{SiH4}SiHX4​ and phosphine PHX3\ce{PH3}PHX3​ show exceptions, indicating that molecular symmetry and lone pair effects must also be considered when evaluating dipole moments.

medium

Identify a limitation of the van Arkel–\text{--}–Ketelaar triangle in predicting the dipole moment of molecules. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Video Solution

fiii

Mark Scheme

molecular symmetry and lone pair effects must also be considered when evaluating dipole moment ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The Van Arkel–\text{--}–Ketelaar triangle categorizes bonding based on percent ionicity and electronegativity difference but does not account for molecular geometry, which is essential in determining dipole moment. Even if a molecule has polar bonds, its overall dipole moment depends on whether the individual bond dipoles cancel due to symmetry. For example, tetrahedral molecules like SiHX4\ce{SiH4}SiHX4​ have polar bonds but no net dipole moment.

Introduction
​

Introduction

Dipole moments are crucial in explaining the physical and chemical properties of molecules. The debye (D) is a unit used to measure dipole moments: 1 D=3.33×10−30 Cm.1\text{ D} = 3.33\times 10^{-30}\text{ Cm}.1 D=3.33×10−30 Cm.

Boiling Point (±2∘C)(\pm 2^\circ\text{C})(±2∘C)

Pauling Model

Linus Pauling devised a formula for the percent ionic character, I,I,I,

I=100×(1−e−Δχ24)I = 100\times \left(1 - e^{-\dfrac{\Delta \chi^2}{4}}\right)I=100×​1−e−4Δχ2​​

where Δχ\Delta \chiΔχ represents the difference in electronegativity.  \newline \
